Calculate peak purity

Source: R/get_purity.R
get_purity.Rd

Estimates peak purity by assessing spectral dissimilarity across the peak region, following Stahl (2003).

Usage

get_purity(
  x,
  pos,
  noise_inflation = 1,
  cutoff = 0.05,
  noise_variance = NULL,
  noise_method = c("quantile", "threshold"),
  noise_quantile = 0.1,
  noise_window = NULL,
  noise_threshold = NULL,
  max_threshold = 0.99,
  background_correction = c("linear", "constant", "none"),
  reference = c("average", "apex"),
  metric = c("fraction", "max"),
  min_run = 3,
  lambdas,
  try = TRUE,
  weight = NULL
)

Arguments

x

A chromatographic matrix (timepoints × wavelengths).

pos

A length-3 integer vector c(apex, start, end) giving the row indices of the peak apex, left boundary, and right boundary in x.

noise_inflation

Multiplier applied to the noise variance, whether supplied via noise_variance or estimated. Values above 1 treat the noise as larger than measured, which loosens the threshold. Defaults to 1.

cutoff

Timepoints at or below cutoff times the background-corrected apex height are excluded, measured at the wavelength of maximum absorbance at the apex. Defaults to 0.05.

noise_variance

Variance of noise. If provided, it replaces the estimate, and the noise_* arguments that control estimation are ignored. Estimating the noise variance requires a pass over the whole chromatogram, so supplying it is much faster when many peaks are assessed.

noise_method

How to select the timepoints used to estimate the noise variance. Either "quantile" (the default), which takes the timepoints in the lowest noise_quantile of maximum absorbance, or "threshold", the legacy behavior, which takes timepoints falling below noise_threshold times the largest absorbance in the chromatogram.

noise_quantile

Quantile of maximum absorbance below which timepoints are treated as noise. Defaults to 0.1.

noise_window

Optional range of row indices to use as the noise region. Takes precedence over noise_method.

noise_threshold

Threshold to define noise, as a proportion of the largest absorbance in the chromatogram. Used only when noise_method == "threshold", where NULL (the default) means 0.005.

max_threshold

Ceiling on the purity threshold. Without it, the threshold approaches one for high signal-to-noise peaks, so the tolerated dissimilarity approaches zero, and spectral variation that noise cannot explain, such as detector non-linearity or a changing solvent composition, makes such peaks impure. Corresponds to the user-defined similarity threshold in the Agilent ChemStation, where 0.99 is a similarity of 990. Defaults to 0.99. Set to 1 to disable.

background_correction

How to correct the peak spectra for background absorbance. Either "linear" (the default), "constant", or "none".

reference

Which spectrum to compare the peak spectra against. Either "average" (the default), the mean of the assessed spectra, or "apex", the spectrum at the peak apex. The apex spectrum correlates perfectly with itself, so it forces a purity ratio of exactly zero at the apex of every peak. Stahl recommends the average spectrum for unknown impurities.

metric

Statistic to summarize the purity ratios. Either "fraction" (the default), the proportion of in-peak timepoints that are pure, or "max", the largest purity ratio. The run-length rule applies to "fraction" only.

min_run

Minimum number of consecutive failing timepoints required to count as impure. Defaults to 3.

lambdas

Wavelengths to include in calculations. Character values are matched to the column names of x; numeric values are taken as column indices. Defaults to all wavelengths.

try

Logical. If FALSE, returns NA without estimating purity. Defaults to TRUE.

weight

The weight argument is deprecated. Please use noise_inflation instead.

Value

Returns the purity of the peak specified by pos: with metric = "fraction", the proportion of timepoints above cutoff not counted as impure; with metric = "max", the largest purity ratio. Returns NA_real_ if the peak cannot be assessed, including when fewer than three timepoints lie above cutoff. An error during the calculation is converted to a warning and also returns NA_real_.

Details

At each timepoint in the peak, the spectrum is compared to a reference spectrum, by default the mean of the assessed spectra. The resulting dissimilarity (\(1 - r^2\)) is divided by the dissimilarity that noise alone could explain, one minus the threshold returned by get_agilent_threshold. A ratio below one means the spectrum is as similar to the reference as the noise permits. With the default metric = "fraction", a timepoint only counts as impure if it belongs to a run of at least min_run consecutive failing timepoints, so isolated failures are ignored. Stahl requires a run of three.

Spectra are background-corrected before comparison by subtracting the spectra at the peak boundaries, interpolated across the peak (background_correction = "linear") or averaged (background_correction = "constant"). Anything that changes linearly across the peak is removed with the background, including a co-eluting impurity much broader than the peak. If preprocess has removed the baseline completely, background_correction = "none" avoids this, but any remaining baseline then enters the comparison as part of each spectrum.

With the default metric = "fraction", pure peaks do not always score exactly one, so treat purity below about 0.9, rather than any value below one, as a sign of impurity. Wide, tailing and weak peaks fall below 0.9 more often than others, even when pure. So do peaks above about 2 AU, whose spectra near the apex are distorted by the detector's non-linear response. The purity calculation is still being refined, and its values may change in future releases.

References

Stahl, Mark. “Peak Purity Analysis in HPLC and CE Using Diode-Array Technology.” Agilent Technologies, April 1, 2003, 16. 5988-8647EN.pdf

Author

Ethan Bass

Examples

data(Sa_warp)
x <- Sa_warp[[1]]
pos <- c(37, 22, 51)
get_purity(x, pos)
#> [1] 0.4545455
